screens.title: Why secure coding matters
screens.narratorSegment: Insecure code often defeats stronger defenses. A hardened network or strong access control cannot stop an attacker who can inject malicious input or hijack a session because the application itself interprets data as commands or trusted tokens. Secure coding means applying disciplined practices — validate inputs, treat untrusted data as data only, and prefer safe libraries that separate code from content. A concrete example: building a web login that concatenates user credentials into a query can allow an attacker to bypass authentication. The safer alternative is a parameterized query where user-supplied values are never interpreted as S Q L. Another example is writing H T M L that includes raw user comments; without encoding, an attacker can execute scripts in other users' browsers. A common misconception is that input validation on the client is sufficient. Client-side checks help UX but cannot be trusted because an attacker can bypass the client. Server-side validation and encoding are non-negotiable. Finally, secure coding is a team responsibility: developers, reviewers, and CI tooling must work together. What practice will you adopt first in your team?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Why secure coding matters
Definition and claim
Secure coding means writing and reviewing code with patterns that prevent untrusted input from becoming executable behavior.
Concrete example
A login using string-concatenated SQL can be bypassed by crafted input. Parameterized queries prevent that class of attack.
Common misconception
Client-side validation is not a security control. All checks must be enforced on the server.
Team practice
Combine secure defaults, code reviews, and automated scans to enforce patterns consistently across the codebase.
Key Takeaway

Treat untrusted input as hostile. Use standard patterns to keep data and code separate.

Analogy & scenario
Think of code as a machine that executes commands. If user data can add new levers, an attacker can control the machine. Secure code locks those levers and only exposes safe controls.
Check your understanding
  • Define why server-side validation is required even with client-side checks.
  • Explain how parameterization prevents SQL injection.
  • Describe when output encoding is necessary for XSS prevention.

screens.title: Injection Flaws (SQL & Command Injection)
screens.narratorSegment: Injection vulnerabilities happen when an application includes untrusted input as part of code or a command. The core issue is a failure to separate code from data. For example, when a database query concatenates a username directly into the S Q L string, an attacker can supply input that changes the query logic. The impact ranges from data exposure to full database compromise. The secure pattern is parameterized queries or prepared statements which send code and data separately to the database driver. An ORM often handles parameterization automatically. A practical misconception is to rely solely on escaping user input; escaping is error-prone and context dependent. Parameterization is deterministic and safer. Concrete example: a login query that uses placeholders and passes user values as parameters. When evaluating code, ask: does user input ever change the structure of a query or command? If yes, refactor to parameters. Finally, adopt automated scans that flag string concatenation used in queries so you catch risky patterns in reviews. Injection Flaws (SQL & Command Injection) means never construct commands with raw user input. use parameterized queries and validated apis to keep data from being executed.. In practical terms, how untrusted input becomes executable instructions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Injection Flaws
What is an injection flaw?
When untrusted input is executed as code or a command, the attacker can change program behavior.
Why parameterization works
  • It keeps the query structure fixed and sends user data separately.
  • Drivers treat parameters as data, not executable tokens.
  • It is less error-prone than custom escaping.
Common Mistake

Using manual string escaping instead of parameterized queries; attackers can bypass fragile escapes.

Key Takeaway

Parameterize queries or use an ORM to eliminate SQL injection risks.

Concrete example
Below is a vulnerable pattern and the secure alternative using parameter placeholders. Read the code and notice how user data is passed separately in the secure version.
# Vulnerable (concatenation)
username = request.args.get('username')
password = request.args.get('password')
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}';"
cursor.execute(query)

# Secure (parameterized)
username = request.args.get('username')
password = request.args.get('password')
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = %s AND password = %s;"
cursor.execute(query, (username, password))
Check
Ask whether any user value can change the command structure. If yes, parameterize or use an API that enforces separation.

screens.title: SQL Injection: Vulnerable Flask example and fix
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll examine a concrete vulnerable Flask snippet and refactor it. The original code constructs an INSERT statement by interpolating user values directly into the S Q L string. This allows an attacker to inject additional S Q L commands or modify the query logic. The safe alternative is to send a parameterized query and pass the user values as parameters to the execute call. In Python's sqlite3 or other DB-A P I drivers, the query uses placeholders like question marks or percent-s specifiers depending on the driver, and the execute method accepts a tuple of values. A common pitfall is to sanitize by hand with string replacement; this is brittle and dangerous. When refactoring, also ensure the connection uses the correct row factory and that commits happen only after validation. The corrected code below shows how to bind parameters and commit safely. As you review code, look for f-strings or string concatenation used in S Q L context and replace them with prepared statements. After you fix code, run a SAST scan to ensure the pattern is not present elsewhere.

keyIdea.title: Refactor rule
keyIdea.text: Replace interpolated SQL strings with parameter binding and avoid hand-rolled escaping; use driver-specific placeholders.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › SQL Injection Fix
Vulnerable Flask snippet
This code uses direct string interpolation to build an INSERT statement.
# Vulnerable section
user_id = request.form.get('user_id')
feedback_text = request.form.get('feedback_text')
conn = get_db_connection()
query = f"INSERT INTO feedback (user_id, text) VALUES ('{user_id}', '{feedback_text}');"
conn.execute(query)
conn.commit()
conn.close()
This pattern allows quotes or SQL fragments in user input to change the statement. Now see the secure replacement which binds parameters and treats user input strictly as data.
# Secure replacement (sqlite3 parameter style)
user_id = request.form.get('user_id')
feedback_text = request.form.get('feedback_text')
conn = get_db_connection()
query = "INSERT INTO feedback (user_id, text) VALUES (?, ?);"
conn.execute(query, (user_id, feedback_text))
conn.commit()
conn.close()
Supporting notes
  • Use the driver-specific placeholder syntax (e.g., ?, %s) for binding.
  • Validate expected types and lengths before inserting into DB.
  • Prefer an ORM when it handles parameterization without raw SQL.
Common mistake
Switching to manual escaping rather than binding parameters. Escaping can be bypassed.
Key Takeaway

Bind parameters and validate inputs. After patching, run SAST to catch similar patterns.

screens.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and Output Encoding
screens.narratorSegment: Cross-site scripting occurs when untrusted data is included in a web page without considering the context in which it will be interpreted. An attacker can inject H T M L or JavaScript and execute it in other users' browsers, leading to session theft or actions performed as the victim. The secure practice is context-specific output encoding: escape H T M L entities when data is rendered in H T M L text, attribute-encode for H T M L attributes, and use JavaScript encoding for values placed inside scripts. Many templating engines provide auto-escaping for H T M L contexts; use those features and avoid disabling them. A common concrete example from Flask and Jinja2 is rendering user feedback directly with {{ item. text }}. Ensuring templates escape output or explicitly calling an escape function prevents script execution. A misconception is that input validation alone stops XSS; in practice you must assume input is malicious and escape on output for the exact rendering context. Finally, use Content Security Policy as a defence-in-depth measure but not as a substitute for proper encoding.

keyIdea.title: XSS rule
keyIdea.text: Always apply context-specific output encoding for untrusted data before rendering it in a page; prefer template auto-escaping.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Reflected XSS example
When the server renders user input directly into HTML, scripts will run in other users' browsers.
Vulnerable template snippet (Jinja2)
<body>
    {% raw %}{% for item in feedback_items %}{% endraw %}
        <p>User ID: {{ item.user_id }}</p>
        <p>Feedback: {{ item.text }}</p> <!-- DANGER: no escaping shown explicitly -->
    {% raw %}{% endfor %}{% endraw %}
</body>
Secure templates enable auto-escaping. If auto-escaping is disabled, apply an explicit escape filter when rendering untrusted text so characters like < and > are converted to entities.
Fixed template
Use the template engine's escape function or ensure autoescape is enabled. Here's an explicit example.
<body>
    {% raw %}{% for item in feedback_items %}{% endraw %}
        <p>User ID: {{ item.user_id }}</p>
        <p>Feedback: {{ item.text | e }}</p> <!-- safe: escaped for HTML -->
    {% raw %}{% endfor %}{% endraw %}
</body>
Pro tip
Enable template auto-escaping for text contexts and apply context-specific encoding when output is used inside attributes or scripts.
Key Takeaway

Encode for the exact context. Template auto-escaping is a powerful first line of defence.

screens.title: Broken Authentication: Risks and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Broken authentication covers a range of failures in how an application verifies identity and manages sessions. Weak password policies, predictable session IDs, missing multi-factor authentication, and verbose error messages can expose accounts to takeover. The secure approach includes strong adaptive password hashing, cryptographically random session identifiers, session invalidation on logout or password change, multi-factor authentication, and generic error messages that do not reveal whether a username is valid. For password storage, use salt plus an adaptive hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt so password verification is costly for attackers. A typical misconception is that TLS alone protects authentication; TLS protects transport but not poor server-side session handling or weak hashes. Also implement brute-force protections and account lockout policies. Finally, design authentication flows so forgotten-password and reset mechanisms do not leak information about registered accounts. These measures collectively reduce the likelihood that an attacker gains or reuses a session. Broken Authentication: Risks and Best Practices means use adaptive hashing, strong session management, mfa, and concise error messages to prevent account compromise.. In practical terms, how weak authentication leads to account compromise and what to do instead. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Broken Authentication
Problem vs Best Practice
Weak: Plain or fast hashing
Using MD5 or SHA1 for passwords stores reversible or fast hashes that attackers can brute force.
Safe: Adaptive hashing
Use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 with unique salts to slow attacker attempts and protect stored credentials.
Session & flow controls
  • Generate cryptographically random session IDs and rotate them on privilege change.
  • Invalidate sessions on logout and after password changes.
  • Implement MFA and rate-limiting to reduce brute force risk.
  • Return generic login errors to avoid username enumeration.
Check your implementation
Review password storage algorithms, session token entropy, and reset flows for information leakage.

screens.title: Insecure Deserialization
screens.narratorSegment: Deserialization converts stored or transmitted data back into in-memory objects. When an application deserializes data from untrusted sources without strict validation, an attacker may craft data that causes unexpected behavior such as instantiating classes, executing code paths, or exhausting resources. The safest approach is to avoid deserializing untrusted input whenever possible. If you must deserialize, restrict types to an allowlist, validate data integrity with signatures or MACs, and run the deserialization logic in a constrained environment. Another mitigation is to use simple, safe formats such as JSON with explicit parsing into plain data structures rather than language-specific binary serializers that can rehydrate objects. A common misconception is trusting serialized data because it came from a cookie or another internal source; always verify origin and integrity. You should also consider limiting resource usage to avoid denial-of-service through large payloads. In secure reviews, flag any deserialization calls and require justification and mitigations in the code change. Insecure Deserialization means avoid deserializing untrusted data. if necessary, restrict allowed types, validate integrity, and prefer simple safe formats.. In practical terms, why deserializing untrusted data can lead to remote code execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Insecure Deserialization
What goes wrong
Deserialization can recreate objects, call constructors, or allocate resources based on attacker-controlled data.
Impact
Remote code execution, authentication bypass, or denial-of-service from crafted payloads.
Safe alternatives
Use JSON and explicit parsing into simple structures, or verify signature and restrict types when necessary.
Practical checklist
  • Avoid language-specific object deserialization of untrusted data.
  • Use allowlists for types and validate payload integrity with signatures.
  • Run deserialization code in a sandbox or limited environment if unavoidable.
Key Takeaway

Prefer safe formats and strict validation; deserialization of untrusted data is high risk.

screens.title: Security Misconfiguration and Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: Security misconfiguration arises when systems run with defaults, unnecessary features enabled, or overly permissive access. Developers and operators must harden applications by disabling debug modes in production, removing unused accounts and services, and restricting access to configuration files and management endpoints. Use infrastructure-as-code with secure baselines so deployments are repeatable and auditable. Automate configuration checks to detect drift and enforce policies in CI/CD. screens.title: Static, Dynamic, and Interactive Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Testing tools extend developer capability by finding patterns humans might miss. Static Application Security Testing inspects source or compiled code without running it. SAST finds injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, and insecure crypto usage early in the pipeline. Dynamic Application Security Testing probes a running application to simulate real attacks and can find issues from component interaction or runtime configuration. Interactive Application Security Testing runs inside the application while it is exercising requests and combines code context with runtime behavior, reducing false positives. Each tool has trade-offs: SAST is fast in CI but can produce false positives; DAST finds runtime issues but requires a running environment and may miss deep code patterns; IAST provides precise diagnostics but needs instrumentation. A robust workflow uses SAST in pre-merge checks, DAST in staging before release, and IAST during higher-fidelity testing for critical services. Triage findings with exploitability and impact to prioritize remediation and avoid developer burnout with low-value findings. screens.title: Secrets, Logging, and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Secrets and logs are frequent sources of data exposure. Never hardcode A P I keys, database credentials, or certificates in source code. Use environment variables, a dedicated secrets manager, or platform-provided key stores to keep credentials out of repositories. For logging, record security-relevant events—authentication attempts, privilege changes, and authorization failures—but redact or avoid logging full secrets and sensitive payloads. Errors should be handled with generic messages in production and detailed diagnostics only in secure internal logs. A common error is sending stack traces to end users or logging entire request bodies that contain credentials. Implement log retention and access controls so forensic data is available to authorized staff without exposing secrets to all teams. Finally, add alerting for unusual patterns such as spike in failed logins or repeated token failures. This combination of secrets management and careful logging improves detection while reducing accidental disclosure. Secrets, Logging, and Error Handling means store secrets in a managed vault, log security events without secrets, and show generic errors to users while retaining internal diagnostics.. In practical terms, protect sensitive data, log useful events, and avoid leaking internal state. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. Avoid committing keys or certificates to source control.

Implement access controls for logs, redact secrets, and enable alerts for anomalous activity like failed login spikes.

fullNarratorScript:
Writing secure code is the single most effective way to reduce application risk. In this chapter you will learn how common vulnerabilities arise, why they matter, and concrete coding patterns to prevent them. We'll use the OWASP Top 10 as a practical checklist, examine real vulnerable Python Flask snippets for S Q L injection and cross-site scripting, and show secure alternatives using parameterized queries and proper output encoding. You will also learn how developers and security teams use static and dynamic analysis tools to find flaws early and how to manage secrets, handle errors, and log security-relevant events safely. By the end of this lesson set you will be able to spot unsafe patterns in code, propose secure fixes, and recommend tooling to automate checks. Think of secure coding as preventive medicine: small changes in how you write and review code stop entire classes of attacks before they reach production. What is one risky pattern you might already find in your codebase?

This chapter has practical, measurable learning objectives. First, you will be able to identify the most common web application risks listed in the OWASP Top 10 and explain the potential impact of each risk on confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Second, you will implement secure coding patterns to prevent injection and cross-site scripting, using parameterized queries and context-specific encoding. Third, you will use static analysis tools in your local development environment or CI pipeline to detect insecure code early. Fourth, you will analyze short code snippets to find insecure patterns and propose concrete, secure alternatives. Each of these skills matters because they move security left in the development lifecycle, reducing the cost and risk of fixes. Practice will focus on reading code, running analysis tools, and pushing small secure fixes with clear commit messages. How would you explain the cost of fixing a security bug found in production versus in a pull request?

Continuing our objectives, you will learn to manage secrets and credentials securely so sensitive keys do not appear in code or repositories. You will also implement secure error handling and logging patterns that record security-relevant events without leaking sensitive information. Next, you will understand insecure deserialization risks and how to avoid remote code execution by validating and constraining deserialized types. Finally, you will practice reading vulnerability reports and proposing prioritized remediations, learning to distinguish urgent, exploitable issues from lower-risk findings. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a milestone to verify competency: a pull request with fixes, a short scan report, or a configuration change. These skills reduce exposure and make incident response faster and more accurate. Which of these objectives would have the biggest effect in your current environment?

Insecure code often defeats stronger defenses. A hardened network or strong access control cannot stop an attacker who can inject malicious input or hijack a session because the application itself interprets data as commands or trusted tokens. Secure coding means applying disciplined practices — validate inputs, treat untrusted data as data only, and prefer safe libraries that separate code from content. A concrete example: building a web login that concatenates user credentials into a query can allow an attacker to bypass authentication. The safer alternative is a parameterized query where user-supplied values are never interpreted as S Q L. Another example is writing H T M L that includes raw user comments; without encoding, an attacker can execute scripts in other users' browsers. A common misconception is that input validation on the client is sufficient. Client-side checks help UX but cannot be trusted because an attacker can bypass the client. Server-side validation and encoding are non-negotiable. Finally, secure coding is a team responsibility: developers, reviewers, and CI tooling must work together. What practice will you adopt first in your team?

Injection vulnerabilities happen when an application includes untrusted input as part of code or a command. The core issue is a failure to separate code from data. For example, when a database query concatenates a username directly into the S Q L string, an attacker can supply input that changes the query logic. The impact ranges from data exposure to full database compromise. The secure pattern is parameterized queries or prepared statements which send code and data separately to the database driver. An ORM often handles parameterization automatically. A practical misconception is to rely solely on escaping user input; escaping is error-prone and context dependent. Parameterization is deterministic and safer. Concrete example: a login query that uses placeholders and passes user values as parameters. When evaluating code, ask: does user input ever change the structure of a query or command? If yes, refactor to parameters. Finally, adopt automated scans that flag string concatenation used in queries so you catch risky patterns in reviews. Injection Flaws (SQL & Command Injection) means never construct commands with raw user input. use parameterized queries and validated apis to keep data from being executed.. In practical terms, how untrusted input becomes executable instructions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll examine a concrete vulnerable Flask snippet and refactor it. The original code constructs an INSERT statement by interpolating user values directly into the S Q L string. This allows an attacker to inject additional S Q L commands or modify the query logic. The safe alternative is to send a parameterized query and pass the user values as parameters to the execute call. In Python's sqlite3 or other DB-A P I drivers, the query uses placeholders like question marks or percent-s specifiers depending on the driver, and the execute method accepts a tuple of values. A common pitfall is to sanitize by hand with string replacement; this is brittle and dangerous. When refactoring, also ensure the connection uses the correct row factory and that commits happen only after validation. The corrected code below shows how to bind parameters and commit safely. As you review code, look for f-strings or string concatenation used in S Q L context and replace them with prepared statements. After you fix code, run a SAST scan to ensure the pattern is not present elsewhere.

Cross-site scripting occurs when untrusted data is included in a web page without considering the context in which it will be interpreted. An attacker can inject H T M L or JavaScript and execute it in other users' browsers, leading to session theft or actions performed as the victim. The secure practice is context-specific output encoding: escape H T M L entities when data is rendered in H T M L text, attribute-encode for H T M L attributes, and use JavaScript encoding for values placed inside scripts. Many templating engines provide auto-escaping for H T M L contexts; use those features and avoid disabling them. A common concrete example from Flask and Jinja2 is rendering user feedback directly with {{ item. text }}. Ensuring templates escape output or explicitly calling an escape function prevents script execution. A misconception is that input validation alone stops XSS; in practice you must assume input is malicious and escape on output for the exact rendering context. Finally, use Content Security Policy as a defence-in-depth measure but not as a substitute for proper encoding.

Broken authentication covers a range of failures in how an application verifies identity and manages sessions. Weak password policies, predictable session IDs, missing multi-factor authentication, and verbose error messages can expose accounts to takeover. The secure approach includes strong adaptive password hashing, cryptographically random session identifiers, session invalidation on logout or password change, multi-factor authentication, and generic error messages that do not reveal whether a username is valid. For password storage, use salt plus an adaptive hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt so password verification is costly for attackers. A typical misconception is that TLS alone protects authentication; TLS protects transport but not poor server-side session handling or weak hashes. Also implement brute-force protections and account lockout policies. Finally, design authentication flows so forgotten-password and reset mechanisms do not leak information about registered accounts. These measures collectively reduce the likelihood that an attacker gains or reuses a session. A common misconception is trusting serialized data because it came from a cookie or another internal source; always verify origin and integrity. In secure reviews, flag any deserialization calls and require justification and mitigations in the code change.
